questions.text:
A schedule of three database transactions [latex]T_1[/latex], [latex]T_2[/latex], and [latex]T_3[/latex] is shown. [latex]R_i(A)[/latex] and [latex]W_i(A)[/latex] denote read and write of data item [latex]A[/latex] by transaction [latex]T_i[/latex], [latex]i = 1, 2, 3[/latex]. The transaction [latex]T_1[/latex] aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

[latex] R_1(X) \quad W_1(Y) \quad R_2(X) \quad R_2(Y) \quad R_3(Y) \quad ABORT(T_1)[/latex]
questions.solution:
Schedule: [latex]R_1(X)\ W_1(Y)\ R_2(X)\ R_2(Y)\ R_3(Y)\ \text{ABORT}(T_1)[/latex].

[latex]T_1[/latex] writes [latex]Y[/latex] before aborting. Any transaction that subsequently read that (now-invalid) value of [latex]Y[/latex] has read "dirty" data and must be cascade-rolled-back:
- [latex]T_2[/latex] executes [latex]R_2(Y)[/latex] after [latex]W_1(Y)[/latex] — it read [latex]T_1[/latex]'s uncommitted write. [latex]T_2[/latex] must roll back.
- [latex]T_3[/latex] executes [latex]R_3(Y)[/latex] afterward too. Since no one else wrote [latex]Y[/latex] in between (only [latex]T_2[/latex] read it, without writing), [latex]T_3[/latex] also reads [latex]T_1[/latex]'s dirty value. [latex]T_3[/latex] must roll back as well.

Answer: Both T2 and T3

questions.text:
A functional dependency [latex]F:X \rightarrow Y[/latex] is termed as a useful functional dependency if and only if it satisfies all the following three conditions:

[latex]X[/latex] is not the empty set. [latex]Y[/latex] is not the empty set. Intersection of [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] is the empty set.

For a relation [latex]R[/latex] with 4 attributes, the total number of possible useful functional dependencies is ______
questions.solution:
X and Y must be non-empty and disjoint. Each of the 4 attributes goes to X, to Y, or to neither: [latex]3^4=81[/latex] ways.

Remove cases with X empty ([latex]2^4=16[/latex]) and Y empty ([latex]16[/latex]); add back both empty (1):
[latex]81-16-16+1=50[/latex]

Answer: 50

questions.text:
The relation schema, Person(pid,city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least 3 persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is
questions.solution:
Without aggregation, "at least 3 persons in a city" means finding 3 different pids with the same city. That needs 3 copies of Person in one tuple:

[latex]\pi_{P1.city}\big(\sigma_{cond}(P1\times P2\times P3)\big)[/latex]
cond: P1.city = P2.city = P3.city and P1.pid, P2.pid, P3.pid all different.

Joining 3 copies needs 2 cross products; with only one cross product we can compare just 2 tuples.

Answer: 2

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the Two Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, so it permits only serializable schedules [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Locking just before each operation and releasing just after violates 2PL (a release followed by a new lock) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Growing phase then shrinking phase: once a lock is released, no new lock can be acquired [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- Deadlock is possible: T1 locks A, T2 locks B, then each waits for the other [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: With 2PL, a transaction always locks the data item being read or written just before every operation and always releases the lock just after the operation
With 2PL, once a lock is released on any data item inside a transaction, no more locks on any data item can be obtained inside that transaction

questions.text: Which of the following file organizations is/are I/O efficient for the scan operation in DBMS?
questions.solution:
A scan reads every record of the file.

- Heap and sorted files store records packed in consecutive pages, so each page is read once [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I/O efficient.
- Unclustered tree / hash index: following the index, records are scattered in random pages; the same page may be read many times (about one I/O per record) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not efficient for a scan.

Answer: Sorted, Heap
